title: "CompStats"
subtitle: "Bootstrap-based statistical comparison of supervised-learning systems evaluated on a shared test set"
toc: false

::: {.home-lead}
**CompStats** is an open-source Python
package for the statistical analysis of the results of supervised-learning systems evaluated on a
shared held-out test set, the setting of collaborative competitions (also called challenges). From
the gold standard and the predictions of each system, it estimates by bootstrap the standard error
and the confidence interval of every performance measure, tests whether the difference between the
best system and each of the others is statistically significant, and corrects those tests for
multiple comparisons.
:::

Competitions rank systems by a point estimate computed on a single test set. The differences
between consecutive systems are often in the hundredths or thousandths. Consequently, a higher
score does not imply that a system would remain better on the population from which the test set
was sampled. Moreover, the statistical tests for comparing learning algorithms require access to
the underlying algorithm [@Dietterich1998], whereas a competition gives access only to the
predictions, and the procedures for comparing classifiers over multiple datasets [@Demsar2006] do
not apply because a competition involves a single dataset.

CompStats implements the methodology of @Nava-Munoz2024, *Analysis of systems' performance in
natural language processing competitions* (Pattern Recognition Letters). The methodology
is designed to complement the standard winner selection process, which in most cases relies solely
on the ranking of the scores, with well-established statistical tools and graphics. It also provides
[measures](pages/methodology.qmd#competitiveness-of-a-competition) that allow organizers to assess
the difficulty of a competition. It is designed to be universally applicable. The article
illustrates it with eight natural language processing competitions as case studies, involving
classification and regression problems.

::: {.pillars}
::: {.pillar}
### Follows the scikit-learn metrics API

A function of `CompStats.metrics` takes `(y_true, y_pred)` like its `sklearn.metrics` namesake and
returns a `Perf` object instead of a float.
:::
::: {.pillar}
### Uncertainty for every measure

The standard error and the percentile confidence interval are computed from the bootstrap
distribution of the measure.
:::
::: {.pillar}
### Paired significance testing

Every system is evaluated on the same bootstrap samples, so the differences are paired. The
p-values come from the bootstrap distribution of the difference, with optional Bonferroni, Holm or
Benjamini-Hochberg correction.
:::
:::

## Quickstart

The package is installed with `pip install CompStats` or with `conda install --channel conda-forge
CompStats`. See [Install](pages/install.qmd) for details. The following example compares three classifiers on
the digits problem.

```python
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
from CompStats.metrics import f1_score

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

svm = LinearSVC(random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
score = f1_score(y_val, svm.predict(X_val), average='macro', name='Linear SVM')
score(RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train).predict(X_val),
      name='Random Forest')
score(GaussianNB().fit(X_train, y_train).predict(X_val), name='Naive Bayes')

score                 # point estimate and standard error of every system
score.ci              # 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals
diff = score.difference()            # paired differences against the best system
diff.p_value(correction='holm')      # p-values adjusted for multiple comparisons
score.plot()                         # performance with confidence intervals
```

## Where to go next

[Install](pages/install.qmd) describes the requirements and the installation methods, and
[Methodology](pages/methodology.qmd) states the statistical basis of the package. The tutorials
are [scikit-learn Users](pages/sklearn_users.ipynb), [Competition
Organizers](pages/competition_organizers.ipynb) and [Multiple
